notes.nedda: Ku is also the word that makes a sentence negative.

guidebook.intro: Lugbara (Lugbarati) is a Central Sudanic language of West Nile, around Arua, Koboko, Maracha and Terego, and of north-eastern DR Congo. It has no noun classes and no verb prefixes: the person is a separate word, so sentences are built from short, unchanging pieces.

tips.title: Mi ngoni?
body: **Mi ngoni?** (how are you?) is the everyday greeting; answer **Ma muke** (I am fine). In the morning ask **Mi ngaa ngoni?** (how did you wake?) and answer **Ma ngaa muke**.
**Awa’difo** is thank you; **Awa’difo amboni** is thank you very much. **Mi mu muke** (go well) is goodbye.

tips.title: Ma, mi, eri
body: The pronouns are **ma** I, **mi** you, **eri** he or she, **ama** we, **emi** you (plural) and **yi** they. They never change: **Ma ni Ayikoru** (I am Ayikoru).
The apostrophe in **a’yo** or **e’yo** marks a catch in the voice (a glottal sound) and is part of the spelling.

culture.title: Greeting in West Nile
body: Greetings matter in Lugbara homes: you greet everyone you meet, ask after the family and thank people at work with **Awa’difo azi ni**. Elders are greeted first.
